chats.title: Can ML weather models predict record heat?

messages.text: I've been running some of the open data-driven global weather models and the headline skill scores are genuinely impressive. But I'm sceptical about one thing: they're trained on roughly forty years of reanalysis, so a heatwave that breaks the record by several degrees is by definition outside what they've seen. Is there any reason to expect a neural network to extrapolate correctly to that, or is it just going to regress toward the training distribution?

Your scepticism is well founded and is an active research question. Neural networks generally interpolate well within the training distribution and can behave poorly outside it. That said, record-breaking events are often unusual combinations of familiar ingredients, such as a persistent blocking high, dry soils, and warm air advection, each of which appears in training data. If the model has learned the dynamics that combine these ingredients, it may produce extreme outcomes even without having seen that exact magnitude. Early case studies show mixed results: some ML models capture the large-scale pattern of record events but underestimate peak temperatures compared with physics-based models.

That matches my gut. The pattern is probably fine, the magnitude is where I'd expect them to fall short. I want to test this properly rather than relying on a couple of cherry-picked case studies. I'm thinking of running hindcasts for every event that set a regional temperature record in the held-out years and comparing peak error against a physics model. Does that design make sense?

It is a solid design. A few suggestions: define events objectively, for instance as exceedance of the prior record at a gridpoint or regional average, so selection is not biased. Evaluate at multiple lead times, since ML models may degrade differently from physics models as lead time grows. Compare against a baseline that is equally out-of-sample, and make sure none of the test years leaked into training or validation. Finally, look at the error conditional on how far the event exceeded the previous record, because the key question is whether error grows with the degree of extrapolation.

I've been generating ensembles from an ML weather model by perturbing the initial conditions, and the spread is way too small. The ensemble mean error is clearly larger than the ensemble spread at most lead times, so the forecasts are overconfident. Is this a known issue with data-driven models, and why would it happen?

Yes, under-dispersion is a widely reported issue. Deterministic ML models trained with a mean-squared-error loss learn to predict something close to the conditional mean, which smooths out small-scale variability. When you perturb initial conditions, the model tends to damp those perturbations rather than let them grow chaotically the way the real atmosphere does. So trajectories converge rather than diverge. Physics-based ensembles also include model-error representations like stochastic parameterisations, which ML models lack by default. The result is a spread-skill ratio well below one, especially at medium-range lead times.

Right, the smoothing makes sense. My spread-skill ratio is around 0.5 at day five and gets worse after that. I'm trying to figure out whether to fix this inside the model, like training it to be probabilistic, or outside it with a post-processing calibration. Retraining is expensive for me so I'm leaning toward post-processing first. What are my options?

Post-processing is a sensible first step. Options include ensemble model output statistics, which fits a parametric predictive distribution using the ensemble mean and spread as predictors with coefficients fitted to minimise the continuous ranked probability score; simple spread inflation with a lead-time-dependent factor; quantile regression or distributional regression with neural networks; and member-by-member methods that rescale deviations from the mean while preserving the ensemble structure. Member-by-member approaches are attractive if you need physically consistent spatial fields for downstream use, since they keep spatial correlations.

Our group shares a cluster with a few dozen GPUs, and most of our work is lots of small training runs, hyperparameter sweeps and ablations that each use maybe a quarter of a GPU's memory. The default scheduler gives each job a whole GPU, so utilisation was terrible. I ended up writing my own scheduler layer that packs several small jobs onto one GPU based on their measured memory and compute footprint. Are there pitfalls I should watch for?

Packing small jobs is a good idea and many groups have done something similar. Main pitfalls: memory estimates can be wrong if jobs have variable batch sizes or memory spikes during evaluation, which causes out-of-memory errors that kill co-located jobs; compute contention can slow each job more than you expect, so total throughput may rise while individual job latency gets worse; and isolation is weak, so a misbehaving job can affect others. Approaches like hardware partitioning on GPUs that support it, or memory caps per process, can help, along with a short profiling run to measure each job's footprint before placement.

I already do a short profiling pass, the scheduler runs each job for a couple of minutes alone, records peak memory and SM utilisation, then bin-packs with a safety margin. Average GPU utilisation went from around 30 percent to over 75 percent and our sweep turnaround dropped a lot. A couple of other labs in the building have asked about it. I'd like to clean it up enough to share, but I'm not sure what documentation people would actually need.

Those are strong results and very shareable. For adoption, people usually need: a quick-start that runs on a single node with a toy workload, an explanation of the profiling and packing logic including the safety margin and how to tune it, a list of assumptions such as supported GPU types and cluster managers, failure modes and how jobs are rescheduled after an out-of-memory error, and a brief summary of your before-and-after utilisation numbers. A short guide for cluster administrators about integrating it with existing fair-share policies would also reduce friction.

I've run the first batch of hindcasts for record heat events. Across about sixty regional records, the ML model gets the location and timing of the heatwave right most of the time at three to five days lead, but underestimates the peak by around two degrees on average, and the shortfall gets bigger the more the event beat the previous record. The physics model underestimates too, but less. How would you interpret that?

That pattern is consistent with the extrapolation hypothesis. If errors grow with the margin by which the record was broken, the model is likely being pulled toward the training distribution, essentially regressing extremes toward familiar values. The fact that location and timing are good suggests the large-scale circulation is captured, while the intensity relies on local processes like land-surface feedbacks that the model may represent poorly at the extremes. The physics model's smaller bias fits with it solving equations that are not bounded by past data. It would be worth checking whether the ML bias is reduced with shorter lead times.

I checked, and at one to two days lead the bias shrinks but doesn't vanish, which actually makes me more convinced it's a magnitude ceiling and not just error growth. I'm cautious about overclaiming though, since sixty events isn't many and they're spatially correlated. I want to make sure I'm not fooling myself.

Good instinct. To strengthen the conclusion, group events by distinct synoptic episodes so that correlated gridpoints from one heatwave do not count as independent samples, and use block bootstrapping over episodes to get confidence intervals. You could also run a placebo test, evaluating the same bias metric on strong but non-record heat events, to check whether the shortfall is specific to out-of-distribution magnitudes. If the bias only appears above the previous record, that is quite persuasive evidence for a ceiling effect.

chats.title: Handling OOM in packed GPU jobs

messages.text: Small issue with my GPU packing scheduler. Occasionally a job's memory spikes way past its profiled peak, usually during validation with larger batches, and it takes down the other jobs sharing the GPU. Right now I use a fixed twenty percent safety margin. Should I make it bigger or is there a smarter approach?

A bigger margin reduces packing efficiency for everyone to protect against a few jobs. Smarter options: profile across both training and evaluation phases, since validation spikes are predictable if you trigger an evaluation step during profiling; set a per-process memory cap so that a spiking job fails alone rather than killing neighbours; implement automatic checkpoint-and-restart so a failed job is requeued on a less crowded GPU with a higher memory estimate; and learn per-job-type margins from history, since repeated runs in a sweep behave similarly.

Profiling an eval step is an obvious fix I somehow missed. I already have checkpoint-and-restart, so adding the per-process cap plus a history-based margin should cover most cases. Honestly this is the kind of practical detail I'd want to pass along to the other labs when I share the tool, because they'll all hit it within a week.

Definitely worth including. A troubleshooting section built from real incidents is often the most valuable part of internal tooling docs. You could also ship sensible defaults, such as profiling with an evaluation step enabled and a modest default cap, so new users avoid the problem without reading anything. Logging which jobs triggered restarts and why will help both you and adopters tune the margins.

I tried ensemble model output statistics on my under-dispersed ML ensemble for two-metre temperature. CRPS improves a lot and the rank histograms are much flatter. But it only works per gridpoint and per variable, and when I look at the calibrated fields they lose spatial coherence. For things like heatwave area or wind across a region that seems like a problem. Am I missing something?

No, that is a known limitation. Univariate calibration fixes marginal distributions at each location but does not preserve dependence across space, time, or variables. The standard remedy is to reorder calibrated samples using a dependence template. Ensemble copula coupling uses the rank order of the raw ensemble members to reconstruct multivariate structure, while the Schaake shuffle uses historical observations as the template. With an under-dispersed raw ensemble, ensemble copula coupling may inherit overly smooth dependence, so the Schaake shuffle or a hybrid can work better for extreme-event metrics.

I hadn't thought about the raw ensemble's dependence structure also being wrong, but that makes sense since it's all too smooth. My worry with Schaake shuffle is that historical templates might not represent the extreme events I care about. I'm starting to think calibration and the extremes question are entangled for me.

They are entangled. Calibration methods fitted on typical days may not hold in the tails, and dependence templates from the past may not capture unprecedented events. You could evaluate calibration separately on the subset of extreme cases, using threshold-weighted CRPS, to see whether calibrated ensembles remain reliable in the tails. Another route is to calibrate with methods that condition on the flow regime, so that blocking situations, for example, get their own correction.

Three groups outside my lab want to try my GPU packing scheduler, and one of them uses a different cluster manager than we do. I'm happy to share the code and walk people through setting it up, it's saved us a huge amount of GPU time. But I'm a bit worried about becoming everyone's unpaid support desk. How do people usually handle sharing internal research tools like this?

A common approach is to open-source the code with a clear license and a statement of support expectations, for example best-effort, issues tracked publicly, no guaranteed response time. Hold a single onboarding session or record a walkthrough so you are not repeating yourself. Encourage adopters to contribute their adapters, such as support for the other cluster manager, back to the repository. Some people also write a short paper or technical note, which gives citable credit and makes the time investment more defensible.

A recorded walkthrough plus a technical note sounds right. I'd actually like it to be a two-way thing, if another lab adapts it for their scheduler I'd learn something too. And frankly, sharing know-how on running lots of small experiments efficiently is something I'm good at and enjoy, more than people might expect from someone who mostly does forecasting.

That is a great position to be in, and it can open collaborations, since groups running many small experiments often have interesting science problems too. You might list the tool and your willingness to advise on research-computing efficiency in your profile or lab page. A small contributors guide that explains how adapters plug in will make two-way exchange much easier.

chats.title: Unusual storm tracks in ML models

messages.text: Extending my extremes analysis beyond heat. I looked at a few storms with really unusual tracks, like a tropical system that turned sharply poleward and reintensified, which is rare in the record. The ML model completely smoothed it into a weaker, more typical track at four days lead, while the physics model caught the turn. Is this the same out-of-distribution problem or something different?

It is likely related but has extra elements. Rare tracks often depend on sensitive interactions, such as a tropical system phasing with a mid-latitude trough, which are underrepresented in training data. ML models trained with mean-squared-error loss also blur intense compact features, so even a well-predicted storm may appear weaker. Both the rarity and the smoothing push toward a typical, weaker outcome. Physics models resolve the interaction explicitly, so they can produce unusual tracks if initial conditions support it.

So for storms I have two confounded issues, smoothing and rarity. I'd like to disentangle them. Maybe compare against common tracks of similar intensity to isolate the rarity effect? I'm still pretty sceptical that these models are ready for warnings on the events that matter most, even though the average scores look great.

Comparing rare-track storms against common-track storms of matched intensity is a good way to isolate rarity. You might also evaluate a probabilistic ML model trained with a proper scoring rule, which suffers less from smoothing, to see how much of the error remains. Your caution about warnings is shared by many operational centres, which currently treat ML forecasts as complementary guidance rather than a replacement for physics models in high-impact situations.

Update on the ensemble calibration. A member-by-member rescaling with a lead-time-dependent inflation factor got my spread-skill ratio from about 0.5 to around 0.95 at day five, and the spatial fields stay coherent because it scales deviations from the ensemble mean. But reliability diagrams for high temperature thresholds still look overconfident. I think calibration works on average and breaks in the tails.

That is a common result. Global inflation fixes the bulk of the distribution, but if the under-dispersion is worse during high-impact regimes, a single factor per lead time will not be enough. You could make the inflation factor depend on predictors such as the ensemble mean anomaly, the flow regime, or the season. Another option is to fit calibration with a tail-weighted score so the optimisation focuses on the thresholds that matter. Check also that your verification sample in the tails is large enough to be confident in the reliability diagram.

State-dependent inflation is my next step. My suspicion is that the model is most overconfident exactly when it's also most biased, during the record events, which would tie back to the extrapolation issue. If that's right, post-processing alone can't fully fix it.

That is a plausible and important point. Post-processing can widen spread and correct systematic bias it has seen, but it cannot recover information the model never produces about unprecedented magnitudes. Showing that overconfidence and bias co-occur on record events would be a strong argument for combining calibration with model-side changes, such as probabilistic training objectives or hybrid physics-ML approaches. A simple scatter of per-event bias against per-event spread-skill ratio would make the case visually.

I'm starting to write up the hindcast study. My main claim is that data-driven weather models capture the large-scale setup of record-breaking extremes but systematically underestimate their magnitude, with error growing with distance beyond the previous record. I don't want it to read as an anti-ML paper, because these models are clearly useful. How would you frame it?

Frame it as characterising a specific limitation to guide development and use. Open by acknowledging the strong average skill, then motivate the question: high-impact decisions depend on the tails, which average scores underweight. Present your evidence as a diagnostic, using the error-versus-exceedance relationship and the placebo comparison with non-record events. Discuss mechanisms like loss-function smoothing and limited training extremes. End with constructive recommendations, such as extreme-focused benchmarks, probabilistic training, and hybrid approaches.

I like the diagnostic framing. I'd also propose a standard extremes benchmark, a fixed set of out-of-sample record events, so model developers can test this themselves. Do you think that's a reasonable contribution or would reviewers see it as scope creep?

It is reasonable if it stays focused. A benchmark is a natural extension of your analysis, since you have already defined events objectively. Keep it minimal: event list, evaluation metrics, and scripts. Reviewers usually welcome reusable resources, especially when existing benchmarks focus on average skill. Make clear the event selection is independent of any particular model to avoid accusations of bias.
